title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
authors: Akinori Machino, Kazuhisa Ogawa, Yuto Ikegai, Takafumi Miyanaga, Koichiro Ban, Nilton F. G. Filho, Hidehisa Shiomi, Toshi Sumida, Shuhei Tamate, Yutaka Tabuchi, Yasunobu Nakamura, Makoto Negoro
abstract: Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large $XX-YY$ interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying $ZZ$ phase. The interaction realizes a 150-ns $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the $XX-YY$ interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.
summary: This paper presents a method to realize high-fidelity, ZZ-free bSWAP gates in superconducting transmon qubits operating in the far-detuned regime. By using a combination of strong driving and a secondary microwave tone, the unwanted ZZ interaction is actively suppressed. This approach demonstrates superior gate performance compared to standard Cross-Resonance techniques, offering a pathway for scalable quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of implementing high-fidelity, ZZ-free two-qubit gates (like bSWAP) in fixed-frequency superconducting transmon qubits while operating in the far-detuned regime.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large XX-YY interaction, and by tuning a weak second tone, the accompanying ZZ phase can be suppressed, yielding high-fidelity gates that outperform Cross-Resonance methods in certain metrics.
method: The analysis uses a multilevel dressed-state theory to derive effective Hamiltonians for the two-qubit interaction, comparing results from the two-level approximation to the full transmon model.
model_or_system: The physical system is superconducting transmon qubits ($Q_A$ and $Q_B$) coupled capacitively. The Hamiltonian is engineered to generate an effective $XX-YY$ interaction while actively suppressing the unwanted $ZZ$ phase using microwave dressing tones.
key_observables: Gate fidelities (IRB/XEB), gate operation times (bSWAP, SWAP, CNOT), and the residual ZZ phase ($\Phi_{ZZ}$).
important_parameters: Drive amplitudes ($\Omega_A, \Omega_B$), detunings ($\delta_A, \delta_B$), and the coupling strength ($g$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the rotating-wave approximation and utilizes a multilevel dressed-state theory to move beyond simple two-level models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup (Stark bSWAP), resonance curves comparing two-level vs. multilevel models, and pulse sequences showing the required two-tone control for ZZ compensation.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical setup and the goal of ZZ-free gate implementation. It then details the Hamiltonian engineering using strong driving and secondary tones to control the ZZ phase. Finally, it compares the performance of the resulting $\sqrt{	ext{bSWAP}}$ gate against established methods like Cross-Resonance, demonstrating speed and fidelity advantages.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of superconducting quantum hardware by providing a robust, high-fidelity gate mechanism that circumvents known limitations (like ZZ crosstalk) inherent in fixed-frequency architectures.
